newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Northern Ireland bombs cloud investment outlook.
newsitem.headline: Northern Ireland bombs cloud investment outlook.

text.p: A car bomb attack on the British army in Northern Ireland may damage the provinces's image overseas, frightening off foreign investors and hitting the key growth area of tourism, economists said on Tuesday.

But they said Monday's double bombing at British army headquarters in one of Britain's best-performing regions should have little impact on a local economy grown impervious to violence after 25 years of conflict.

The bombing, the most serious guerrilla attack in Northern Ireland since the ceasefires of 1994, came as the province's business leaders gathered in Pittsburgh for a U.S. conference on trade and investment.
Teir attempts to build closer links with U.S. firms and to highlight the potential for inward investment will be hampered by the violence, the economists said.

"Investors, even from the Pacific Rim who are less risk averse than most, will not even look at this place while there is political instability never mind bombs going off," said Michael Smyth, senior lecturer at the University of Ulster.
Northern Ireland's business community is also worried.

"Anything that lessens the perception of Northern Ireland is dmanaging and won't help matters," said one Belfast business source. "Up to now, people could talk about a de-facto ceasefire in Ireland but that is clearly not the case anymore."
Tourism, the main beneficiary of the 1994 ceasefires, is another area likely to suffer from the bombing.
"Obviously developments like the ending of the ceasefire and what happened yesterday do have their impact," said Philip McDonagh, principal economist at Coopers & Lybrand in Belfast.
"They impact on the tourism industry as anybody planning to visit the province will be having second thoughts."
The number of holiday visitors to Northern Ireland soared by 68 percent in 1995 as tourists took advantage of peace to visit the region.
"From our point of view, it's a setback," said Mo Durkan, spokesperson for the Northern Irish Tourist Board. "But it's certainly by no means the most major setback we've ever had."
The violence is also likely to affect the export market for Northern Ireland goods as purchasers become more nervous about buying there.
"Even where there might be no foundation for it, the perception is there may be difficulites about reliability of supplies and so on," Cooper & Lybrand's McDonagh told Reuters.

But economists say Monday's bombs should have little direct effect on a resilient underlying economy which has outperformed most other regions of Britain in terms of output growth and productivity, household income and employment in recent years.

"If there was to be a resumption of violence, it wouldn't affect the underlying performance of the economy because for 20 years now, those few firms that we have here have been able to find ways of coping with this," Smyth said.
"The effect is on opportunities missed, the opportunity cost, like in tourism or inward investment, what might have been."
Smyth says the mad cow crisis, which has badly hit Northern Ireland's agriculture sector, poses a far more serious threat to the local economy than Monday's bombs.
"It has hit the rural economy, it is hitting agriculture machinery suppliers, it's hitting hauliers. It'll take a while for that to feed through to job losses but it will," he says.
